result.summary: Pausanias traces the early history of the Olympic games, from Clymenus and Endymion through Pelops, Hercules and Iphitus. He then lists the events added over time, with their first winners.

scenes.title: Mythic founders of the games
scenes.summary: Clymenus, Endymion, Pelops, Amythaon, Pelias and Neleus, Augeas and Hercules each hold games at Olympia. Early winners are named, and the games lapse after Oxylus.

scenes.title: Events added after Iphitus
scenes.summary: After the revival under Iphitus, the Eleans gradually added events. Pausanias names each event's first winner, from Corœbus to Phædimus.

alias_notes.explanation: Tradition says Aethlius's father Æolus was surnamed Zeus.
Cretan Hercules, one of the Curetes, distinguished from the Theban Hercules.

notable_quotes.reason: Shows how the revived games recovered their ancient programme piece by piece.

analysis.text: Pausanias shows the games as an evolving institution, blending myth and recorded history, with founders giving way to dated victors.
Dating by Olympiads and listing winners from many cities reflects how Greeks reckoned time and civic pride through athletics.

legacy.text: Olympiad lists like these became the basis of Greek chronology and influenced the modern Olympic Games.

fun_facts.text: Belistiche, a woman from Macedonia, is recorded as an Olympic victor as a chariot owner, as owners rather than drivers won.

language_notes.text: Deucalion's flood is the Greek myth's great deluge; Pausanias uses it as a starting point for dating the earliest mythic events.
Curetes: divine attendants linked with the infant Zeus on Crete; here Idæan Hercules is one of the Idæan Dactyls, not the son of Amphitryon.
"Æolus surnamed Zeus" means Aethlius was said to be the son of Zeus by way of a tradition that identified Æolus with Zeus.
The sentence is awkward: it means the only victors Hercules crowned were those listed, Iolaus winning with Hercules' borrowed mares.
Riding race: a race on horseback, distinct from the chariot race.
Pancratium: a brutal combined contest of wrestling and boxing with very few rules.
The "double course" (diaulos) was a race of two stadium lengths, down the track and back.
"Wild olive crown" refers to the victor's prize at Olympia, a wreath cut from the sacred wild olive tree.
The pentathlum was a five-event contest; the traditional events were running, jumping, discus, javelin and wrestling.
The pancratium combined boxing and wrestling with very few restrictions.
"307th Olympiad" is evidently a textual error; the boys' contests were introduced in the 37th Olympiad.
The race in heavy armour (hoplitodromos) was run by men carrying a shield and wearing a helmet.

context_notes.text: Pelops was the hero for whom the Peloponnese is named; his chariot-race victory is the traditional story behind the Olympic games.
Homer's Iliad Book 23 describes the funeral games for Patroclus, including a chariot race in which Menelaus drives Agamemnon's mare Æthe.
Castor and Pollux were the twin Dioscuri, sons of Zeus or Tyndareus, famed as horseman and boxer respectively.
Iphitus of Elis was the king traditionally credited with reviving the Olympic games, conventionally dated to 776 BC.
Smyrna was a city on the coast of Asia Minor, held at different times by Aeolians and Ionians.
Crannon was a city in Thessaly, a region famous for its horses.
Belistiche's victory is notable because women could not compete as athletes; they could win in equestrian events as owners.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias offers an antiquarian aside, justifying the borrowed horses as a custom of the heroic age and showing his habit of explaining the past through Homer.
The flat, chronicle-like closing sentence compresses a long lapse into one clause, typical of Pausanias' catalogue style.
The games are described almost as a memory slowly returning, as if the festival itself were recovering from forgetting.
Pausanias distances himself from a local legend, showing his habit of reporting tradition while openly doubting it.
